title: Heedlessness, the forgetting
hook: forgetting Allah in the rush of the day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road of lying, and your line: truth leads to good. Where did a small lie try to slip out, and what did you say instead? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

Alarm. Coffee. Inbox. Car. Meeting. Lunch at the desk. Another meeting. Traffic. Dinner. Phone. Sleep. Nothing in that day was wrong. No one was lied to, nobody was envied, no temper was lost. And still, somewhere in it, the thing the Qur'an calls heedlessness may have happened. It isn't a sin anyone sets out to commit. It's a remembering that gets skipped, all day, without anyone noticing. Today's word: ghaflah, heedlessness, the forgetting.
screen: `A DAY WITH NOTHING WRONG.` → `A REMEMBERING SKIPPED.` → `GHAFLAH.`

segments.voice: Start with a verse that names the cure and the disease together. The Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to remember his Lord within himself, humbly and with awe, at morning and evening, and it ends, in Pickthall's words: "And be not thou of the neglectful." The Arabic word there is al-ghafilin, the heedless. Morning and evening: remembering is placed at the edges of the day, the very times a rush begins and ends. Second, what forgetting does. Another verse warns against being like those who forgot Allah, so that he made them forget themselves. Forgetting Allah, in that verse, isn't a small gap on a schedule. It comes with losing track of your own soul. Third, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari puts it starkly: the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. Not good and bad. Awake and not. Which is why the carry today is wake up. And last, the shape of the cure. Heedlessness isn't fixed by one long session. It's fixed the way sleep is interrupted: by small bells through the day. The call to prayer. The words said on waking, before eating, on leaving the house. Each one is a tap on the shoulder, for a day that, left alone, forgets.
screen: `AT MORNING AND EVENING.` · `FORGOT ALLAH, FORGOT THEMSELVES.` · `THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.` · then, large: `SMALL BELLS THROUGH THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: set a reminder to remember. After the bell, pick up your phone, or a sticky note, and choose a time in the middle of today, the busiest part. For now, settle, and breathe. Decide what the reminder will say. One word is enough: Allah, or wake up, or the name of something you're grateful for. Decide what you'll do when it goes off: one breath, one line of a remembrance you already know, one look out a window. If you pray, you can ask not to be among the heedless. The bell holds the time.
Ghaflah. Heedlessness: forgetting Allah in the rush of the day; in the Qur'an, the neglectful. Today's word.

Your line: wake up. Set the reminder, and when it goes off, do the one thing you chose, even in the middle of a sentence. Tomorrow, the last disease of the heart: despair, the closed door. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims counter ghaflah, heedlessness, with dhikr, the remembrance of Allah, built into the day through the prayers, the call to prayer, and short remembrances said on waking, eating and leaving home.

original.note: Arabic: heedlessness, neglectful forgetting; the Qur'an speaks of al-ghafilin, the heedless.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgetting God for a day is no big deal if you did nothing wrong.
what it means: ghaflah is the forgetting itself; the Qur'an warns against being among the heedless.
what a scholar hears: 7:205's morning-and-evening remembrance, 59:19's forgetting of self, and al-Bukhari's living and dead.
